_note: Three research themes. 'description' paragraphs and 'summary' are edited by hand; 'keywords' decide which papers appear under each theme; 'featured' are the DOIs shown on the research page.

themes.name: Genomic selection and breeding design
themes.summary: How genomic and phenotypic information can be used to predict genetic merit, and how breeding programs can be designed to turn those predictions into sustained genetic gain.
description: The advent of genomic selection has accelerated genetic progress in dairy cattle and other livestock species, and much of our work concerns how that progress can be sustained in practice. We evaluate which genotyping and phenotyping strategies are worth their cost, whether additional information such as gut microbiome composition improves the prediction of complex traits, and how well predictions hold across populations and production systems. The traits we study range from meat quality and carcass composition in pigs to longevity and fertility in dairy and beef cattle. Statistical methods for genomic prediction and fine-mapping are developed in close collaboration with colleagues in statistical genomics at NC State.

Prediction is useful only when a breeding program can act on it. We therefore also study program design, including how genotyping strategies, mating plans, germplasm exchange, and selection decisions balance genetic gain against the loss of genetic variation. Much of this work relies on large, routinely recorded datasets, such as producer-recorded health events and national genotype collections.

themes.name: Inbreeding and genetic diversity
themes.summary: How inbreeding can be measured from genomic data, what it costs in performance, health, and fertility, and how selection can be managed to preserve genetic variation.
description: Preserving genetic diversity is necessary if livestock populations are to remain responsive to future breeding goals, yet intense selection concentrates genetic contributions on a limited number of families. We use genomic data, and runs of homozygosity in particular, to measure inbreeding more precisely than pedigrees allow and to follow how inbreeding and diversity have changed in dairy and beef breeds in North America, Europe, and Australia.

A second line of work concerns the cost of inbreeding. We estimate inbreeding depression for production, fertility, health, and longevity, separate the effects of recent and ancient inbreeding, and look for the genomic regions responsible. These estimates inform the mating and selection strategies we evaluate, such as genomic inbreeding penalties and planned germplasm exchange, which aim to sustain genetic gain while curtailing the loss of variation.

themes.name: Host genome, microbiome, and resilience
themes.summary: How the host genome and the gut microbiome jointly shape performance, and how animals respond to heat stress under a changing climate.
description: The performance of an animal reflects both its own genome and the microbial communities it carries, and the host genome contributes to shaping those communities. Working mainly in pigs, we estimate how much of the variation in gut microbiome composition is under host genetic control and how much of the variation in growth, feed efficiency, and carcass traits the microbiome accounts for. We also test whether microbial information improves the prediction of those traits alongside genomic data.

Heat stress poses a growing threat to livestock production and welfare, a problem exacerbated by climate change. In sows genomically selected for heat tolerance, we combine automatically recorded body temperature, time-resolved microbiome and other omics data, and genomic information to characterize how animals respond to heat and how selection can improve their resilience.
